comments.author: @kevinmoore8780
comments.text:
One aspect not mentioned in the video is what are the view plains from the site?  Especially view plains if trees were removed.  Having a military structure among trees might have some purposes but if it was a site to protect from a rear attack then there had to be a viewing advantage.  On many forts the view can be hard to envision.  A great example was the Prince of Wales Tower in Point Pleasant Park that for decades had its view of the harbour blocked by pine trees.  The only good thing about the lose of pines at the park during Juan was you could see the harbour again from the Tower.    So if the Bayer Lake walls were meant to be temporary military protection, thus no mortar, then the soldiers hiding behind them would have to be facing some logical approach for enemies.

Nova Scotia is full of old structures.  Sometimes hard to go hiking and not stumble over some foundation or wall.  Outside of Nova Scotia there are some anti-aircraft structures that were built but never even equipped with cannon so late in the wear.  They had "log cannons" instead.  Many old roads in Nova Scotia have walls running along them.  When the road was made, the rocks moved were made into walls and not just thrown into piles.  Sometimes you have to wonder why the people making the road took the time to do that but it was a common practice.

I think from the data provided in the video that the walls are likely from the last 100 years.  Nothing found at the site is older and there is nothing to use for carbon dating.  So until something or some way is found to date the site then we have to assume it is more recent than older.

replies.author: @HiddenCanada
replies.text: The sightlines are a useful point, Kevin, especially what approaches would have been visible without today’s trees. That could help test the military explanation. One distinction, though: the recent artifacts date activity at the site, not necessarily the walls’ construction. They don’t establish that the walls are under a hundred years old. Thanks for the thoughtful comment.

comments.author: @dac762-n9v
comments.text: Just a note: lichen is no longer considered a valid dating methodology, and was only ever used for very rough estimates anyway. Furthermore, it’s was generally only used/usedul at northern sites.

replies.author: @dac762-n9v
replies.text: @HiddenCanada no, sorry, no reference. I’m just recalling my time working as an archaeologist up north. We didn’t use lichen as a matter of course so I never did read the primary documents. As I recall, the general basis for rejecting lichen dating was twofold: the inherent error when measuring lichen samples in the field (they’re not uniform in size, even in the same rock), and the difficulty in accurately inferring growth rates over long time periods. It may be used in some contexts, but those would be very old sites where those issues are less significant.

replies.author: @HiddenCanada
replies.text: The limitations matter here. I mention that the examiner and method weren’t documented, so that estimate doesn’t settle the walls’ age. Do you have a reference for the broader claim that lichen dating is no longer considered valid?
